title: "VITRAL: A target centric system for knowledge management in conflict environments"
author: Rodrigo Fileto Cuerci Maciel

# Introduction
Small and medium-sized law enforcement agencies face severe operational friction when reconciling evidence collected across fragmented intake channels—such as CCTV footage, call detail records, and automated license plate scans. Rather than a lack of raw information, the primary bottleneck is cognitive overload caused by static, siloed database systems that force analysts to manually connect disparate data points. Grounded in Robert M. Clark’s Target-Centric Intelligence paradigm, this paper addresses this challenge by presenting an open-source reference software architecture and micro-ontology. The system decouples event ingestion from core graph representation, organizing incoming observational data into a dynamic, target-centric knowledge graph without requiring proprietary software licenses or complex infrastructure.

# Theoretical Foundations and Related Work
Modern intelligence-led policing requires shifting from traditional entity-centric tracking—which focuses on isolated suspects—to target-system modeling, which captures the broader web of relationships, assets, and operational nodes. While relational databases enforce rigid schemas that break when new data types are introduced, graph-based knowledge representations provide the flexibility needed to model complex, evolving criminal networks. This section reviews the convergence of intelligence frameworks and semantic graph technologies, identifying a key gap in current systems: the lack of a lightweight, open-source reference architecture that bridges multi-source event ingestion with a standardized, auditable micro-ontology for local law enforcement.

# Design Science Research Methodology
This research follows the Design Science Research Methodology (DSRM) for information systems, aiming to design, instantiate, and evaluate a software artifact that solves a defined operational problem. Based on operational requirements identified in municipal police workflows, we formulate five core Design Requirements ($\text{DR}_1$–$\text{DR}_5$): target-centric graph structuring, source-agnostic intake, confidence-gated event filtering, dual operational modality (asynchronous batch and synchronous streaming), and immutable provenance tracking. These requirements directly govern the structural design and technical evaluation of the reference architecture.

# The Reference Architecture & Micro-Ontology
The core artifact consists of an event-driven reference architecture centered on an extensible RDF/Turtle micro-ontology. To ensure schema flexibility across varied sensors, all incoming data is abstracted into a core tid:Observation class, which links ephemeral events (e.g., visual detections, license plate captures, telecommunication logs) to persistent entity nodes (tid:TargetPerson, tid:Vehicle, tid:PhoneNumber). The architecture incorporates a confidence-gated mechanism ($\tau_{\text{high}}, \tau_{\text{low}}$) that automatically commits high-confidence observations to the primary graph while routing ambiguous events to a human-in-the-loop verification queue, preserving graph cleanliness and evidentiary chain-of-custody.

# System Instantiation
To demonstrate the feasibility of the reference architecture, we developed a functional open-source prototype using an asynchronous Python backend. The system combines an API ingestion layer (FastAPI), an event queue manager (Redis/Celery) for background processing, and a graph storage engine executing openCypher queries over an in-memory graph database (Memgraph). This decoupled stack allows small police forces to deploy the system on standard, low-cost hardware while maintaining the capability to scale background workers as incoming video or log files increase.

# Synthetic Demonstration & EvaluationEvaluating the system without ethical review constraints requires a fully non-human, deterministic testbed. We map the multi-camera perspectives of the publicly available Market-1501 benchmark dataset to spatial sensor nodes within the graph, supplementing them with synthetic license plate and call detail records tied to the dataset's identities. The evaluation benchmarks system ingestion throughput, graph query response latency across multi-hop traversals, and the mathematical efficiency of the confidence-gating engine in reducing analyst queue volume.

# Discussion and Operational Boundaries
The evaluation results confirm that the reference architecture satisfies the initial design requirements, offering a scalable substrate for target-centric intelligence analysis. By abstracting data intake into standardized event structures, the platform significantly reduces manual data handling for analysts while maintaining a strict audit trail of automated commits and manual edits. This section also discusses operational boundary conditions, including hardware constraints in small departments, dependency on feature extractor quality, and the deliberate exclusion of complex automated analytics from this baseline architecture.

# Conclusion and Future Research
This paper contributes an open-source, target-centric reference architecture and micro-ontology designed to streamline intelligence management for resource-constrained law enforcement agencies. By providing a standardized blueprint for event ingestion and graph-based target representation, the artifact offers a flexible foundation for modern intelligence-led policing. Future work will extend this baseline architecture by introducing specialized analytics modules, including complex network metrics for structural network disruption and automated cross-jurisdictional graph federation.

# Conceptual Framework and Literature Review

Forensic Intelligence bring the concept of trait

information as thing [@buckland1991] and information as evidence

Further, the term “evidence” implies passiveness. Evidence, like information-as-thing, does not do anything actively. Human beings do things with it or to it. They examine it, describe it, and categorize it. They understand, misunderstand, interpret, summarize, or rebut it. They may even try to fake it, alter it, hide it, or destroy it. The essence of evidence is precisely that perception of it can lead to changes in what people believe that they know.
